intro: Day 2 of SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 ran in three slots: 10:00 AM, 1:30 PM and 5:00 PM. The morning paper was reported as easy to moderate, the 1:30 PM paper drew mixed reports (mostly easy to moderate), and the 5:00 PM paper was reported as the hardest of the day, with Quant (long Data Interpretation sets) the main problem while Reasoning and English were easy. These reviews come from candidate interviews on YouTube, candidate surveys and coaching-site analyses, and all figures are unofficial. One survey-based video said no papers were scheduled for 2, 3 and 4 October, so the next analysis will be added when exams resume; that break is reported by one source and is not confirmed by SSC here. The 15-minute locked timer for each section remains the main talking point.

shifts.summary: Candidates called the morning paper easy to moderate, in line with the shifts held on 30 September. Reasoning and English were the easier sections. GA was moderate, with more static GK than current affairs. Quant was mostly Advanced Maths (mensuration, geometry, algebra) with some calculation-heavy arithmetic, and it was the section where the timer hurt most. Candidates also described a few questions as repeats of previous-year patterns. Reports about a few out-of-syllabus statistics questions come from one survey video and are not confirmed.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Mostly standard types, with coding-decoding, analytical reasoning and series. A few questions were long. Non-verbal reasoning had a large share (about 5–6 questions), and analogy and classification had about 4–5.

topics.topic: Non-verbal: mirror and water images, paper cutting and folding, embedded figures

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: More static GK than current affairs. About 15 questions were reported as comfortably doable. Several questions were on the Constitution and the economy.

topics.topic: Articles of the Constitution (243, 131A) and the 97th Amendment

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: About 70% was Advanced Maths and about 30% arithmetic. The arithmetic was calculation-heavy, and about 2–3 questions were long. Reviewers said it was the section where time ran short. One reviewer estimated about 20 questions as easy.

topics.topic: Geometry: circles, chords and tangents, centroid

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: Vocabulary was largely based on previous-year patterns. The passage was reported as a little easier than usual. One-word substitution appeared in sentence form. The grammar covered voice and narration.

asked.q: Who was the first Indian to win a Grand Slam title? (as recalled by candidates)
Questions on IMEC (the India–Middle East–Europe corridor) — about 2 questions.
A question on Chapchar Kut, the festival of Mizoram.
A question on the Booker Prize.
Questions on Article 243 and Article 131A.
A question on the 97th Constitutional Amendment (cooperative societies).
Questions on the BNS / BNSS, including zero FIR.
A question on the year of the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri.
A question on the Digboi refinery.
A question on the 18 Puranas.
A question on Manu Bhaker.
A question on Kho Kho at the South Asian Games.
A question on the novel 'Train to Pakistan'.
A question on the vegetation of the Eastern Ghats.
3–4 questions on circles (chords, tangents), a centroid question and an alternate-day work problem.

observations: Quant is where the timer hurt most: time lost on calculation-heavy arithmetic cannot be recovered after the 15-minute lock.
Candidates mentioned no systemic technical problems. One video reported that some candidates were turned away at entry because of an Aadhaar biometric lock issue.
A candidate survey (275 responses) reported an average of about 87 attempts and an average score near 148. The sample is small and skewed to engaged test-takers.
disagreements: Overall difficulty: Moderate on CareerPower and Mission Gyan, Easy to Moderate on Testbook, PW and most candidate videos.
Good attempts: 79–83 on CareerPower and in candidate interviews, 75–82 in one video and 74–84 on one listing. All are unofficial.
Quant topics: one reviewer said there was no statistics or probability, while another recalled a statistics (median) question. The sources do not separate shifts clearly.
Some sources mix up shifts, since a few sites call the 1:30 PM paper 'Shift 1' for 30 September. The reports used above are the ones labelled 1 October.

shifts.summary: Reviews of the afternoon paper are fewer and more mixed. Candidate interviews and one analysis called it easy to moderate, with Reasoning simple and Quant formula-based, and some candidates reported 87–92 attempts. Other listings rate it Moderate or harder. English had a tricky spot-the-error set, and the reading passage was reported to match a popular mock passage. Treat these figures as early and unconfirmed.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Reported as simple and doable in about 13–14 minutes. It had coding-decoding, series and an AP-type question. One stacked-box puzzle confused some candidates.

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: Mostly one-line questions across polity, history and economy. Reports disagree on current affairs: one candidate said there were almost none, while others recalled a few appointment and index questions.

topics.topic: Acts and Articles of the Constitution

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: About 22–23 questions were reported as doable and mostly formula-based. Reviewers said 15–16 of them resembled previous-year or sectional mock patterns.

topics.topic: Geometry: circles (about 3), hexagon in a circle, tangents
Profit & loss, time & work, SI/CI, partnership

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: It had cloze, direct and indirect speech, active and passive voice, synonyms and antonyms, idioms and one-word substitution. The reading passage was reported to be identical to one in a popular mock. Spot-the-error was the trickiest set.

observations: One candidate said they were allotted a centre far from home despite their city preference. This is a single account.
A candidate reported the platform lagging; it is unclear whether that was the exam platform or a mock site.
disagreements: Difficulty: candidate interviews and one analysis say Easy to Moderate, one listing says Moderate and another says Moderate to Difficult with only 66–78 good attempts.
Reasoning: most reviews say simple, but one survey video reported low average marks. That video may mix shifts from 30 September and 1 October.
Quant topics: one reviewer said there was no circle and no DI, while candidates in other interviews reported circle questions.

shifts.goodAttempts: Not reliably reported (survey average about 83–84 attempts)
shifts.summary: The evening paper was reported as the hardest of the day and, like the 30 September evening shift, leaned towards the difficult side. Reasoning and English were described as easy, and Quant was the problem: long Data Interpretation sets, lengthy calculations and a few odd geometry questions, all under the 15-minute lock. General Awareness reports conflict, from tough to no major problems. The figures come from self-selected candidate surveys and a few candidate videos, so treat them as early and unconfirmed.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Called the easiest section of the shift. About 4 statement-based questions (assertion, implicit-assumption type), about 4 series questions, 3 odd-one-out questions, one dice question and one age question. Counting figures (a triangle with many small triangles) took time. One of the statement questions was described as debatable.

topics.topic: Odd one out (including a GK-flavoured set of river and mountain names)
Non-verbal: counting figures, odd figure out

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: Reports disagree. One candidate called it tough, with guesswork needed after about 14–15 questions, while a survey-based review said there were no major problems. Questions were a mix of static GK and a few conceptual questions, with about 3–4 on current affairs.

topics.topic: History: Pitt's India Act 1784 (asked for the month) and a question on books
Current affairs: an appointment and BIMSTEC

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: The section that changed the shift. Candidates reported 4–5 Data Interpretation questions, with small charts that were hard to read on small screens, plus lengthy calculation and a few geometry questions that took time. One candidate said most algebra questions involved decimals but the options were whole numbers, so shortcuts did not help. Reviewers said the DI sets were solvable but slow to read, and the 15-minute lock made it worse.

topics.topic: Geometry: equal chords and the central angle, incentre angle sum
Mensuration: hemisphere volume to radius, cone
Algebra: a−b and powers (a to the power 6), decimal-based
Profit and loss (selling price and cost price)

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: Described as based on previous-year patterns. It had active and passive voice, 2 narration questions, about 4 vocabulary questions (a spelling, a meaning, an antonym and a homonym), 2 easy error-spotting questions, a moderate tense-based cloze test and 2 sentence-rearrangement (PQRS) questions, one of them tricky.

asked.q: In which month did Pitt's India Act of 1784 come into force? (as recalled by a candidate)
A question matching Sahitya Akademi Award winners with their languages.
A question asking which language belongs to the Indo-Aryan family.
A question on Myanmar joining BIMSTEC.
A question on the pollutants measured in India's Air Quality Index (which of four options is not one of the 8).
2 questions on LPG reforms, and one on the term for the government selling a public enterprise (privatisation).
A question on the doping principle applied to athletes (a candidate recalled the answer as strict liability, not verified).
4–5 Data Interpretation questions, about 3 geometry questions (equal chords, incentre), a hemisphere question and a cone question.

observations: Quant is where the shift was lost: reviewers said the lock of 15 minutes per section and the time spent reading DI sets cut attempts sharply.
Candidates reported that on smaller exam screens the DI charts and options appeared zoomed and needed scrolling. This is a centre-level report and does not apply to everyone.
A candidate who attempted 88 questions said about 4 of 20 General Awareness attempts were wrong and expected 8–9 wrong overall. This is one self-reported account.
SSC normalises scores across shifts, so a harder evening shift is expected to be balanced against easier ones.
disagreements: Overall difficulty: realmocks survey respondents rated it harder than last year (66% Difficult, 4% Easy, 31% Same, 572 responses), and the RBE survey found 59% Difficult (215 responses). One site's Shift 3 listing says Easy for repeaters and Easy to Moderate for freshers, but its figures match the Shift 2 summary and look copied.
General Awareness: one candidate called it tough, while the RBE review said no major problems and good attempts.

Attempts: survey averages are about 83–84 attempts (realmocks 83.4, average marks 134.79; another listing 83.3 and 134.76). These are self-reported averages from engaged test-takers, not good-attempt estimates.
Quant attempts: RBE reported an average of about 16 attempts in Quant, which is a survey figure and was not found in other sources.

faqs.q: What was the difficulty level of SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 on 1 October?
faqs.a: Shift 1 was reported as easy to moderate, with 79–83 good attempts. Shift 2 was mostly called easy to moderate, with some mixed reports. Shift 3 was reported as moderate to difficult, mainly because of a hard Quant section.

faqs.q: How many good attempts were there on 1 October 2026?
faqs.a: For Shift 1, about 79–83 out of 100. Shift 2 reports range from about 80 to 90, though some listings say lower. For Shift 3 there is no reliable good-attempts estimate; survey averages are about 83–84 attempts. These are unofficial estimates.

faqs.q: Which Shift 1 General Awareness questions were asked on 1 October?
faqs.a: Candidates recalled questions on IMEC, Chapchar Kut, the Booker Prize, Articles 243 and 131A, the 97th Amendment, the BNS/BNSS and zero FIR, and the first Indian Grand Slam winner. These are memory-based and unofficial.

faqs.q: Is the 15-minute sectional timer still in force?
faqs.a: Yes. Each section locks after 15 minutes and you cannot return to it, so skipping long questions early is important, especially in Quant.

faqs.q: Will a tougher shift lower my final score?
faqs.a: No. SSC normalises scores across shifts, so candidates in a harder shift are not penalised compared with those in an easier one.
